rationale: A wins because it keeps the holes visible instead of turning them into drama; its line "which national pharmacy chain (not named in the facts - must not be invented)" is exactly the discipline this update needs. B has a sharper broad-business swing with "The poster child of online-only retail now runs more than 300 stores," but it leans on a history and thesis the supplied facts do not prove. The difference is small, but A is less likely to get the founder embarrassed on the first reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker bets its next 40 stores on the optometrist" overstates the fact pattern slightly; the update says most new stores will offer exams, not all 40.
"LensCrafters, EssilorLuxottica, Pearle Vision" imports specific competitor context that was not supplied. It may be true, but this exercise asked for tight grounding.
"retail-health category" is a real lens, but A admits "without it, this is a one-company observation, not yet a trend." That means the angle is not fully pitch-ready without outside examples.

A misses the cleanest broad retail story: the company crossing 300 stores after being framed around online commerce. It gestures at "glasses-by-mail disruptor" but does not make the DTC reversal its own angle.
gaps_in_B: "poster child of online-only retail" and "canonical example" are strong copy, but they are not in the supplied update. That is a borrowed reputation, not a provided fact.
"won't say what the exams earn" turns "exam-revenue contribution not broken out" into a refusal. A markets reporter can interrogate the omission; do not imply evasiveness unless you have it.
"Warby's founding pitch was eliminating the middleman" and "pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" import outside narrative. Useful if verified, sloppy if not.
"category-creation" is inflated. Warby adding optometrist-staffed exams is a retail-health or service-expansion story, not category creation.
